detailed_rationale:
Aarti Industries is a large, diversified specialty and commodity chemicals maker (Nitro Chloro Benzenes, Di-Chloro Benzenes, Phenylenediamines, Nitro Toluene derivatives, sulphuric acid and 100+ products) with major facilities across Gujarat and Maharashtra. The headline concern in the data is capital efficiency: ROCE has deteriorated sharply, from a historical 19-20% down to around 7% currently, alongside a meaningful rise in debt (Rs 3,623 Cr to Rs 4,966 Cr, Mar 2024 to Mar 2026) -- a classic 'capex ahead of returns' pattern for a company that has been investing heavily through a period when Chinese oversupply has pressured specialty and commodity chemical pricing across the Indian industry, not just at Aarti.

The more encouraging signal is the sequential recovery visible in the last five quarters: net profit has climbed steadily from Rs 43 Cr (Jun 2025) to Rs 106 Cr, Rs 133 Cr, Rs 137 Cr and Rs 155 Cr (Jun 2026), alongside modestly improving margins (13% to 16% OPM) -- consistent with capacity utilization gradually improving and/or a sector pricing bottom. FY26 revenue grew to Rs 8,286 Cr from Rs 7,271 Cr (+14%) with profit up to Rs 419 Cr from Rs 331 Cr (+27%), so the full-year trend is already positive even if the return-on-capital metric has not yet caught up.

At a PE near 43-44x, the valuation is not cheap for a business whose ROCE has fallen to single digits, so the market is implicitly betting on continued sequential margin/return recovery; we would want that recovery to keep showing up before treating the stock as anything better than a Hold.
recommendation_rationale: Hold, matching the quant score -- the sequential profit recovery over the past five quarters is real and worth crediting, but capital efficiency (ROCE ~7%, down from 19-20% historically) has genuinely deteriorated alongside rising debt, and the current multiple does not look cheap enough to reward that combination with anything more constructive than a Hold.
summary: Aarti Industries, a large diversified specialty and commodity chemicals manufacturer, has seen its return on capital fall sharply (from a historical high-teens level to around 7%) as debt rose to fund capacity expansion during a period of industry-wide pricing pressure from global oversupply. The last five quarters do show a steady sequential profit recovery, and FY26 overall revenue and profit both grew at double-digit rates. We rate it a Hold: a real recovery is underway, but capital efficiency has not yet caught up, and the valuation is not undemanding.
positive_para: Profit has grown sequentially for five straight quarters (Rs 43 Cr to Rs 155 Cr), FY26 revenue and profit both grew at double-digit rates, and Aarti remains one of India's larger diversified specialty-chemical platforms with scale across multiple product lines and manufacturing sites -- a real base to recover from as sector pricing stabilizes.
negative_para: Return on capital employed has fallen from a historical 19-20% to around 7%, a genuine deterioration in capital efficiency, while debt has risen roughly 37% over two years to fund the capacity behind that lower-return base -- this is a real fundamental concern, not a data artifact, and specialty/commodity chemical pricing pressure from global (particularly Chinese) oversupply remains a sector-wide risk outside the company's control.
reverse_dcf_judgment: At roughly 43-44x earnings against a ROCE that has fallen to about 7%, the multiple is pricing a meaningful return-on-capital recovery that has not yet fully shown up in the numbers, even though the sequential profit trend is moving the right way. This is a 'show me' valuation: reasonable if the last five quarters' recovery continues and broadens into improved capital efficiency, rich if the current single-digit ROCE proves closer to the new normal for this capex cycle.
